entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q1
entry.itemBody: What will be the effect on a direct exchange rate quote if the domestic currency appreciates?

feedback.neutral: B is correct. In the case of a direct exchange rate, the domestic currency is the price currency (the numerator) and the foreign currency is the base currency (the denominator). If the domestic currency appreciates, then fewer units of the domestic currency are required to buy one unit of the foreign currency, and the exchange rate (domestic per foreign) declines. For example, if British pound sterling (GBP) appreciates against the euro (EUR), then euro –sterling (GBP/EUR) might decline.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q2
entry.itemBody: An executive from Switzerland checks into a hotel room in Spain and is told by the manager that EUR1 will buy CHF1.2983. From the executive’s perspective, an indirect exchange rate quote would be:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. An indirect quote takes the foreign country as the price currency and the domestic country as the base currency. To get Swiss francs —which is the executive’s domestic currency—as the base currency, the quote must be stated as EUR/CHF. Using the manager’s information, the indirect exchange rate is (1/1.2983) = 0.7702.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q3
entry.itemBody: Over the past month, the Swiss franc (CHF) has depreciated 12 percent against the British pound (GBP). How much has the pound sterling appreciated against the Swiss franc?

feedback.neutral: C is correct. The appreciation of the British pound against the Swiss franc is the inverse of the 12 percent depreciation of the Swiss franc against the pound sterling: [1/(1 – 0.12)] – 1 = (1/0.88) – 1 = 0.1364, or 13.64%.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q4
entry.itemBody: An exchange rate between two currencies has increased to 1.4500. If the base currency has appreciated by 8 percent against the price currency, the initial exchange rate between the two currencies was closest to:

feedback.neutral: B is correct. The percentage appreciation of the base currency can be calculated by dividing the appreciated exchange rate by the initial exchange rate. In this case, the unknown is the initial exchange rate. The initial exchange is the value of X that satisfies the formula: 1.4500/X = 1.08 Solving for X leads to 1.45/1.08 = 1.3426.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q5
entry.itemBody: In the classification of currency regimes, a currency board system (CBS) most likely differs from a fixed-rate parity system in that:

feedback.neutral: B is correct. In a CBS, the monetary authority has an obligation to maintain 100% foreign currency reserves against the monetary base. It therefore cannot lend to troubled financial institutions. As long as the country under a fixed parity regime maintains its exchange peg, the central bank can serve as a lender of last resort.

choices.itemBody: A. a CBS can peg to a basket of currencies but a fixed-rate system cannot.
B. the monetary authority within a CBS does not act as a traditional lender of last resort.
C. a CBS has a discretionary target level of foreign exchange reserves.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q6
entry.itemBody: The most likely reason for a country to encourage foreign direct investment while heavily restricting foreign investment in liquid domestic assets is to:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. Capital flight occurs when foreign investment in liquid domestic assets suddenly decreases. Restricting foreign investment in liquid domestic assets and encouraging foreign direct investment (i.e., investment in illiquid domestic assets) prevents capital flight.

choices.itemBody: B. generate an increase in the domestic interest rate.
C. stabilize the production capacity of the domestic country. Capital Flows and the FX Market Faculty: Page 2 of 6

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q9
entry.itemBody: Which of the following is most likely a characteristic of a country that follows the dollarization exchange rate regime? The country:

feedback.neutral: B is correct. When a country adopts the US currency as its currency, hence the name dollarization, the dollarized country inherits the currency credibility of the US dollar.

choices.itemBody: A. is able to monetize its domestic debt.
B. has the currency credibility of the US dollar.
C. has a term structure similar to that of the United States.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q10
entry.itemBody: An analyst gathers the following information: Foreign inflation rate 2% Domestic inflation rate 3% Change in nominal exchange rate 6% Note: the exchange rate is expressed as the number of units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency. The change in the real exchange rate is closest to:

feedback.neutral: B is correct. because the change in the real exchange rate is (1 + ΔSd/f/Sd/f) × (1 + ΔPf/Pf) / (1 + ΔPd/Pd) − 1 = (1 + 6%) × (1 + 2%)/(1 + 3%) − 1 = 1.06 × 1.02/1.03 − 1 = 0.0497 ≈ 0.05 = 5%, where ΔSd/f/Sd/f is the change of the nominal exchange rate, ΔPf/Pf is the foreign inflation rate, and ΔPd/Pd is the domestic inflation rate. Using the appropriate approximate formula, 6.0% + 2.0% – 3.0% = 5% leads to the same answer choice.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q11
entry.itemBody: When a country has a fiscal surplus and an excess of private saving over investment, its exports are:

feedback.neutral: C is correct. because using a fundamental identity from macroeconomics, the relationship between the trade balance and expenditure/saving decisions can be expressed as: X– M = (S – I) + (T – G) where X represents exports, M is imports, S is private savings, I is investment in plant and equipment, T is taxes net of transfers, and G is government expenditure. From this relationship, we can see that a trade surplus (X > M) must be reflected in a fiscal surplus (T > G), an excess of private saving over investment (S > I), or both. We can also see that when a country has a fiscal surplus (T > G) and an excess of private saving over investment (S > I), its exports are greater than its imports (X > M).

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q12
entry.itemBody: The conversion of nominal exchange rates into real exchange rates requires the:

feedback.neutral: B is correct. because real exchange rates, which are indexes often constructed by economists and other market analysts to assess changes in the relative purchasing power of one currency compared with another. Creating these indexes requires adjusting the nominal exchange rate by using the price levels in each country of the currency pair.

choices.itemBody: B. price levels in both countries. Capital Flows and the FX Market Faculty: Page 3 of 6

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q13
entry.itemBody: Price levels increase by 2% in the US and by 6% in the Eurozone. If the nominal spot exchange rate of the USD/EUR (amount of US dollars per 1 euro) decreases by 4%, the absolute change in the real exchange rate is closest to:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. because the change in the real exchange rate is (1 + Δ𝑠𝑑/𝑓 𝑠𝑑/𝑓 ) × (1 + Δ𝑃𝑓 𝑃𝑓 ) (1 + Δ𝑃𝑑 𝑃𝑑 ) − 1 (1 − 4%)× (1 + 6% 1 + 2%) − 1 ≈ 0% Thus, the change in the real exchange rate is approximately zero percent. The rough calculation is: −4% + 6% − 2% = 0%.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q14
entry.itemBody: An ideal international currency regime would most likely have:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. because the ideal currency regime would have three properties. One of those properties is, all currencies would be fully convertible (i.e., currencies could be freely exchanged for any purpose and in any amount). This condition ensures unrestricted flow of capital. Capital Flows and the FX Market Faculty: Page 6 of 6

choices.itemBody: C. a common monetary policy across different countries.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q15
entry.itemBody: In contrast to real exchange rates, nominal foreign exchange rates:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. because nominal exchange rates exhibit persistent deviations from PPP.

choices.itemBody: A. tend to deviate from purchasing power parity.
B. represent the relative price levels in the domestic and foreign countries.
C. are indexes useful for understanding international trade and capital flows.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q16
entry.itemBody: Which of the following economic conditions for a country best supports a well-functioning currency board exchange rate system?

feedback.neutral: A is correct. because a currency board system works best if domestic prices and wages are very flexible. 17. . A is correct because in case of dollarization the country uses the currency of another nation as its medium of exchange and unit of account.

choices.itemBody: B. Rapid growth in supply of the global reserve asset
C. Large non-traded sectors of the domestic economy

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q17
entry.itemBody: Dollarization is best described as an exchange rate regime whereby a country:

choices.itemBody: A. uses the currency of another nation as its medium of exchange.
B. participates in a monetary union whose members share the same legal tender.
C. makes a commitment to exchange domestic currency for a specified foreign currency at a fixed exchange rate.

entry.title: 2027 Economics Mod7-Q18
entry.itemBody: Assume that the nominal spot exchange rate (USD/EUR) increases by 7.5%, the eurozone price level decreases by 4%, and the US price level increases by 2.5%. The change in the real exchange rate (%) is closest to:

feedback.neutral: A is correct. Real exchange rate = Nominal spot exchange rate × (CPI of the foreign country/CPI of the domestic country) Change in the real exchange rate = [(1 + Change in exchange rate) × (1 + Change in price level in foreign country)]/(1 + Change in price level in domestic country) – 1 = [(1 + 7.5%) × (1 – 4%)]/(1 + 2.5%) – 1 = 0.7%.
